runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as a risk area in its own right, covering how training data, model outputs, and inferences can expose personal information.

**Core risks.** The profile opens its data privacy section by noting that GAI system training requires large volumes of data, which in some cases may include personal data. It then says that the use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose specification.

**Transparency and memorization.** The profile observes that most model developers do not disclose specific data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identifiably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected. It also warns that during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. This problem has been referred to as data memorization, which may create heightened privacy exposure even for data that appears in only a few training samples.

**Inference.** Beyond memorized content, GAI models may be able to correctly infer PII or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. The profile notes that these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations).

**Harm categories.** The profile lists harms from information exposure (such as extortion or dignitary harm), and says wrong inferences about PII can contribute to downstream or secondary harmful impacts.

**Where data privacy sits in the framework.** Data privacy appears in the profile's risk taxonomy across categories: it is listed among risks that are Misuse by humans (or malicious use) and among Ecosystem / societal risks (or systemic risks). The profile also says some risks are cross-cutting between these categories.

**Suggested actions.** The profile's suggested actions include monitoring for exposure, such as to conduct periodic monitoring of AI-generated content for privacy risks; to establish policies for collection, retention, and minimum quality of data, including for Leak of personally identifiable information, including facial likenesses of individuals. Another suggestion is to consider opportunities to responsibly use synthetic data and other privacy enhancing techniques in GAI development, so that the data matches real-world statistics without disclosing personally identifiable information or contributing to homogenization.

The search did not cover the profile's full set of privacy-enhancing techniques beyond these actions, so this answer reflects the passages retrieved.

segments.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as a risk area in its own right, covering how training data, model outputs, and inferences can expose personal information.

**Core risks.** The profile opens its data privacy section by noting that
GAI system training requires large volumes of data, which in some cases may include personal data.
It then says that
the use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose specification.
**Transparency and memorization.** The profile observes that

most model developers do not disclose specific data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identifiably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.
It also warns that
during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. This problem has been referred to as data memorization

, which may create heightened privacy exposure even for data that appears in only a few training samples.

**Inference.** Beyond memorized content,
GAI models may be able to correctly infer PII or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources.
The profile notes that
these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations)

.

**Harm categories.** The profile lists
harms from information exposure (such as extortion or dignitary harm)
, and says wrong inferences about PII
can contribute to downstream or secondary harmful impacts.
**Where data privacy sits in the framework.** Data privacy appears in the profile's risk taxonomy across categories: it is listed among risks that are
Misuse by humans (or malicious use)
and among
Ecosystem / societal risks (or systemic risks)
. The profile also says
some risks are cross-cutting between these categories.
**Suggested actions.** The profile's suggested actions include monitoring for exposure, such as to
conduct periodic monitoring of AI-generated content for privacy risks;
to
establish policies for collection, retention, and minimum quality of data
, including for
Leak of personally identifiable information, including facial likenesses of individuals.
Another suggestion is to
consider opportunities to responsibly use synthetic data and other privacy enhancing techniques in GAI development
, so that the data matches real-world statistics
without disclosing personally identifiable information or contributing to homogenization.

The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as a risk area in its own right, covering how training data, model outputs, and inferences can expose personal information.

**Core risks.** The profile opens its data privacy section by noting that GAI system training requires large volumes of data, which in some cases may include personal data. It then says that the use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose specification.

**Transparency and memorization.** The profile observes that most model developers do not disclose specific data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identifiably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected. It also warns that during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. This problem has been referred to as data memorization, which may create heightened privacy exposure even for data that appears in only a few training samples.

**Inference.** Beyond memorized content, GAI models may be able to correctly infer PII or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. The profile notes that these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations).

**Harm categories.** The profile lists harms from information exposure (such as extortion or dignitary harm), and says wrong inferences about PII can contribute to downstream or secondary harmful impacts.

**Where data privacy sits in the framework.** Data privacy appears in the profile's risk taxonomy across categories: it is listed among risks that are Misuse by humans (or malicious use) and among Ecosystem / societal risks (or systemic risks). The profile also says some risks are cross-cutting between these categories.

**Suggested actions.** The profile's suggested actions include monitoring for exposure, such as to conduct periodic monitoring of AI-generated content for privacy risks; to establish policies for collection, retention, and minimum quality of data, including for Leak of personally identifiable information, including facial likenesses of individuals. Another suggestion is to consider opportunities to responsibly use synthetic data and other privacy enhancing techniques in GAI development, so that the data matches real-world statistics without disclosing personally identifiable information or contributing to homogenization.
